clue.text: One-time passcode that might make sense, a poem

indicators.note: What letters MIGHT make is not what they already spell, so the words beside it are raw material to be built with rather than read.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters — exactly the length the grid wants

explanation.surface: Somebody wondering whether a one-off login code could be read as a short piece of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Arabian Nights magic worked exactly like a one-time passcode: say the words once and the rock opens. Counting settles the parse, since 'sense, a poem' is ten letters and nothing else is.
explanation.definitionFit: Open sesame is the phrase that swings the robbers' cave door in the Arabian Nights, and it works only for whoever knows it — a passcode.

clue.text: Somewhat upfront? I'm early! Not late, anyway …

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the following words' letters is taken

parts.note: the letters run across upfront, I'm and early

explanation.surface: Someone protesting that they arrived ahead of time, so certainly not late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' signals a run of letters inside 'upfront? I'm early'; 'anyway' just rounds off the surface as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Arriving at the scheduled moment means being punctual, the opposite of tardy.

clue.text: Yet, really — knight to take place of queen?

indicators.note: one letter taking the place of another means it replaces it in the word

parts.note: ever so, as in 'ever so kind', means really
R, for Regina, is the abbreviation for a queen
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A chess player wondering whether a knight could really stand in for the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess setting suggests Q for queen, but here queen is R (Regina). In EVER SO ('really'), N ('knight') is 'to take place of' that R.
explanation.definitionFit: Even so means nevertheless or however, the conjunction sense of the short word given.

clue.text: Ill-tempered; also ingratiating — thankfully concise

parts.note: being short with somebody is being curt and snappish
both words do nothing but add the next thing on
sweet in the sense of sugary charm laid on to please

explanation.surface: A character sketch of somebody snappish one minute and oily the next, delivered briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: The punctuation is the disguise: a semicolon and a dash make three unrelated synonyms look like one continuous description of a person's manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Short and sweet describes something mercifully brief and pleasant with it, so the relief in 'thankfully' is part of the phrase's meaning rather than decoration.

clue.text: Bird generally dull in appearance? That's rough, as Aussie tells it

indicators.note: An Australian broadens the vowel in words like paper and mate, so a word said in that accent lands on a sound English spells another way.

parts.note: the rough stuff you rub bare wood down with is sandpaper, and that is the word being said aloud

explanation.surface: Somebody sympathising about a tough time, in a broad Australian accent.
explanation.walkthrough: Australian vowels are the whole mechanism: 'mate' comes out as 'mite' down there, and the same shift turns a hardware-shop abrasive into a wading bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandpipers are the small shoreline waders got up in browns and greys, so 'generally dull in appearance' is a fair sketch of the whole family.

clue.text: Audio kit invariably preceding Novembers?

definitions.note: Kit is a mass noun covering any number of pieces at once, so a phrase that looks singular fairly defines a plural answer.
definitions.meaning: the studio sense: the things singers and broadcasters talk into
the radio-alphabet sense: M comes before N, so the word standing for M always comes before the word standing for N

explanation.surface: A stage manager checking that the sound gear is always in place before the autumn shows.
explanation.walkthrough: The NATO alphabet is the second definition: pilots and police say Mike for M and November for N. 'Invariably' is the word telling you a fixed rule is being quoted rather than a coincidence.
explanation.definitionFit: Mikes are microphones, the working name for them in any studio; and in the NATO spelling alphabet Mike is the letter before November every single time.

clue.text: Spouse scratching backside stopped by a ragamuffin

indicators.note: A backside is the rear end, and scratching it out here means the letter at the back is rubbed away.
Being stopped by something means it gets in your way, so the letter named is planted inside the word rather than added at either end.

parts.note: the married partner, the female one
the letter of the word 'a' itself, dropped into the gap behind the opening letter

explanation.surface: A spouse caught scratching an itch, interrupted by a scruffy child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backside' is anatomy on the surface and a position in the wordplay, and that one word does all the misleading in a four-letter clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A waif is a thin, uncared-for child adrift with nobody to claim them, which is the ragged street urchin 'ragamuffin' names.

clue.text: After outburst (anger), Dad served up drinkie

indicators.note: Serving something up presents it back to you the other way about, and in a down entry that means the assembled letters are read from the bottom upwards.

parts.note: a fit is a sudden outburst of temper
ire is anger, and the setters' favourite three letters for it
pa is the familiar word for a father

explanation.surface: Dad, having lost his temper, pouring the drinks out afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(anger)' looks like the setter glossing the word in front of it, and it is a separate piece of wordplay with three letters of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperitif is the small drink taken before dinner to sharpen the appetite, and 'drinkie' is the coy diminutive for exactly that sort of glass.

clue.text: Weld, insulate and earth aeroplane's body

parts.note: to fuse two metals is to weld them into one
in Britain you lag a hot-water tank or a pipe — wrap it against the cold
E is the earth terminal marked inside a plug

explanation.surface: A list of workshop instructions for somebody assembling something in a hangar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lag' is worth learning for good: British setters reach for it whenever insulation appears in a clue, and it never means anything else.
explanation.definitionFit: The fuselage is the long central tube of an aircraft, carrying crew and cargo with the wings bolted to it — an aeroplane's body exactly.

clue.text: Primarily trademarked aerobic exercises, boogieing occasionally?

definitions.text: Primarily trademarked aerobic exercises, boogieing occasionally?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so what is wanted from each of the words that follow is the letter it opens with.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the three words, taken in order
the opening letter of each of the last two words, which finishes the entry

explanation.surface: A fitness class sold as branded aerobics with a bit of dancing thrown in now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word after the first hands over its initial, and the sentence they spell is itself a fair description of the thing — a clue with no separate definition anywhere in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tae-Bo is Billy Blanks's trademarked workout, taekwondo kicks crossed with boxing, so the sentence also reads straight as a description of it.

clue.text: Raw beside Loch — because of this under kilt?

indicators.note: Beside puts one thing alongside another, so the two pieces are simply written next to each other in the order the clue gives them.

parts.note: raw in the sense of bare and uncovered, as raw flesh is
Loch Ness is the Highland lake with the monster, and setters use the second half of its name on its own

explanation.surface: Something raw sitting by a Scottish loch, and the old question about what is worn under a kilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loch' is a definition by example running backwards: the setter names the category and expects the most famous instance of it, which is how crossword lochs, rivers and dukes all work.
explanation.definitionFit: Tradition insists a true Scot wears nothing beneath the kilt, so what is under there is bare skin — nakedness.

clue.text: Drinkin' G&T in which a little slice (lime?), where the powerful are

parts.note: downing means drinking, here with its final G dropped as the apostrophe shows

indicators.note: in which means the following letters are placed between the G and T

parts.note: the letters G and T from the drink's name

indicators.note: a little of the word slice is just its first letter

parts.note: first letter of slice
a lime is a kind of tree; the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: Someone downs a gin and tonic with a sliver of lime in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drinkin'' is DOWNIN', minus its G. S (a little of 'slice') plus TREE (a lime is a tree) goes inside G and T to give GSTREET.
explanation.definitionFit: Downing Street in London is home to the British Prime Minister and the seat of government.

clue.text: Overturning favourite sofas, gutted, Everyman's making a gaffe

indicators.note: Overturning a thing tips it end over end, so the whole run of letters just built is read back from its far end.
Something gutted has had its insides taken out and only the shell left, which for a word means its first and last letters.

parts.note: a favourite is a pet — the teacher's pet
the middle is taken out and the two outer letters of the word are left
the setter signs himself Everyman, so 'Everyman is' is him saying I'm

explanation.surface: The setter admitting he has tipped his favourite sofas over and wrecked them.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman writes himself into his own clues: whenever the name appears it is the setter speaking in the first person, so it is worth a pronoun rather than a search for a proper noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A misstep is a wrong move, and in ordinary speech a blunder of conduct rather than of walking — which is what a gaffe is.

clue.text: Bird noticed notice

parts.note: the past tense of see
a bill pasted on a wall is a public notice — hence billboard

explanation.surface: Somebody spotting a poster.
explanation.walkthrough: Three words, two of them near-identical: 'noticed' and 'notice' read like a typo and are two entirely separate pieces of vocabulary.
explanation.definitionFit: A sawbill is a merganser, the fish-eating duck whose beak carries serrated tooth-like edges, so 'Bird' names it by class.

clue.text: Fried pig in peanuts, hardly savoury

indicators.note: Something dropped into hot fat comes out changed in shape, so the letters beside the word do not keep the arrangement they arrived in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters — the full length of the entry

explanation.surface: A pig fried in peanuts, which is not a dish anybody is queueing for.
explanation.walkthrough: Surface and definition agree with each other for once — the dish really does sound horrible — and that agreement is what stops you noticing that 'in' belongs to the letters rather than to the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Unappetising means it puts you off eating it, and 'hardly savoury' says the same by understatement — the food is not tempting.

clue.text: Pop Idol Jack in trashed hotel, sonny, stripped off

indicators.note: a trashed hotel room is wrecked, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: J is the card abbreviation for jack
taken as written

indicators.note: stripped off means the outer layer, the first and last letters, is removed

parts.note: sonny without its outer letters

explanation.surface: A rock star's son trashes a hotel room and strips naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripped off' leaves ONN from sonny; J (Jack), HOTEL and ONN are 'trashed' together into the singer's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Elton John is a hugely famous pop star, a musical idol for decades; the clue's capitals hint at the TV show.

clue.text: Gathered that man, clumsy fellow, to be given upside-down cake?

indicators.note: Turning a thing upside-down puts its bottom at the top, so the short word beside it is written out in reverse.

parts.note: pud is the British shortening of pudding, the dessert course a cake can serve as, and it is turned round
calling somebody a great ape is calling them a lumbering oaf
the pronoun for a man already mentioned

explanation.surface: A clumsy man being handed a slice of pineapple upside-down cake.
explanation.walkthrough: Upside-down cake is a real thing — the pineapple sort baked in an inverted tin — and that is what makes the two words look like one noun rather than an instruction and the word it operates on.
explanation.definitionFit: Something heaped up has been piled into a mound, which is what gathered means when it is things rather than people being brought together.

clue.text: Did Amy and Ted never stop getting bling?

definitions.note: a noun: showy jewellery, matching the noun answer

indicators.note: never coming to a stop means none of the four words reaches its final letter

parts.note: did with its last letter cut off, never reaching its stop
the name Amy with its last letter cut off
the word and with its last letter cut off
the name Ted with its last letter cut off

explanation.surface: A gossip asking whether a couple kept on acquiring flashy jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'never stop' drops the last letter (D, Y, D, D) of each of Did, Amy, and, Ted, leaving DI, AM, AN, TE.
explanation.definitionFit: Diamante is cheap sparkling decoration of paste or sequins, exactly the flashy jewellery called bling.

clue.text: Plan for how to get out: try flailing with axes, get it?

definitions.text: Plan for how to get out

indicators.note: flailing means thrashing wildly, so the letters are thrown about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone trapped is told to hack a way out with axes; do they understand?
explanation.walkthrough: 'flailing' acts on TRY, AXES and GET IT together; 'with' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An exit strategy is a prepared scheme for leaving a situation, such as a war or investment.

clue.text: Courage? That's not on tap

definitions.meaning: the slang sense: the nerve to go through with something frightening
the pub sense: beer sold sealed in glass rather than pulled from the pump

explanation.surface: A drinker being told the good stuff is not available on draught tonight.
explanation.walkthrough: Courage is a long-established British brewery as well as a virtue, which is why the surface reads as a bar conversation while the definition is talking about nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottle is British slang for nerve — losing your bottle is losing your nerve — and beer that is not drawn from a tap is served in one.

clue.text: Clip of broadcast, Rally of the Stars

indicators.note: A clip is a short piece cut out of something longer, so what is wanted is a run of letters taken from inside the words that follow.

parts.note: six letters in a row, beginning inside the first word and finishing inside the second

explanation.surface: A trailer for a televised motor race with a celebrity line-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Rally of the Stars' look like the title of a programme, so the eye takes it as one unit and skims straight over the join where the letters sit.
explanation.definitionFit: Astral means belonging to the stars — astral bodies, astral navigation — so the phrase is the adjective's plainest sense.

clue.text: Classical city of Greek character wherein I mope about

indicators.note: wherein means in which, so the next letters go inside the Greek letter

parts.note: pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

indicators.note: about means around in a muddle, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Greek character in a story moping around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' is the letter PI, not a person; 'about' shuffles I and MOPE into OMPEI, and 'wherein' puts that between P and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Pompeii is the Roman town buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, a city of classical antiquity.

clue.text: Where a house-warming will get you a frosty reception

definitions.meaning: the surface sense: the party you throw when you move in
the surface sense is a cold welcome from the neighbours; the setter means the walls, which are built out of the cold itself

explanation.surface: New neighbours throwing a party and finding nobody much wants to come.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the phrase turn literal at the same moment: warming the house really would be a disaster, and the reception really is frosty because the building is made of snow.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is a dome of snow blocks, so warming the house would melt it, and a frosty welcome there is nothing but the temperature.

clue.text: Fancies new liniments, scratching head

indicators.note: The head of a word is its first letter, and scratching it means rubbing that letter out before the rest is used.

parts.note: n = new, the standard abbreviation
a liniment is a rubbing lotion for aching muscles

explanation.surface: Somebody scratching their head over which new rubbing ointment to buy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratching head' works twice over: it is the puzzled gesture in the picture and, in the wordplay, the instruction to rub a first letter out.
explanation.definitionFit: Notions are passing ideas taken up on a whim, which is what fancies are when they are things thought rather than things desired.

clue.text: Artist's party welcoming concerning amateur archer

indicators.note: Welcoming somebody is taking them into your house, so the word beside it opens up and the rest of the wordplay goes inside.

parts.note: a do is a party in British usage — a works do, a birthday do
a book on birds is a book concerning birds
a = amateur, the standard abbreviation
William Tell shot the apple off his son's head

explanation.surface: A painter's party making room for a keen weekend bowman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Archer' wants to be the definition and is wordplay instead, and it points at a Swiss folk hero rather than at anybody holding a bow — Tell is the setters' standard archer.
explanation.definitionFit: Donatello was the Florentine sculptor of the bronze David and one of the founding figures of the Renaissance, so 'Artist' names him by trade.

clue.text: With no entrance, tenant to go in

indicators.note: An entrance is the way in, so the letter standing at the way into the word — the first one — is the letter taken away.

parts.note: somebody who rents a flat is a renter, and a tenant is exactly that

explanation.surface: A flat with no front door, and a tenant expected to get inside somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' does the disguising: a doorway on the surface, the front of a word in the wordplay. 'Tenant' looks like the definition right up to the moment you count the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a room is to go into it, so this is the plainest possible synonym — the same act stated in three words instead of one.

clue.text: Loudly plead for Merlin's victim?

indicators.note: Said out loud a word is only a sound, and this one turns out to be spelt a different way when it is written down.

parts.note: to plead with heaven is to pray, and it is that word said aloud that gets written down

explanation.surface: Somebody begging noisily for mercy from a wizard.
explanation.walkthrough: Merlin is a wizard on the surface and a bird in the parse: the merlin is a compact falcon, and the capital letter is doing all the misdirecting.
explanation.definitionFit: A merlin is a small falcon, and what a hawk hunts and kills is its prey — the wizard in the surface is the decoy.

clue.text: Poor — and potentially sole-destroying?

definitions.meaning: the everyday sense: shabby, worn, short of money
the literal sense: heels that have gone take the bottom of the shoe with them

explanation.surface: Hard times described as bad news for your footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sole-destroying' is a pun on soul-destroying, so the second definition arrives disguised as a complaint about how demoralising being broke is.
explanation.definitionFit: Down-at-heel means shabby and hard up, and shoes worn down at the heel are on their way through the sole — the pun being on soul-destroying.
